summary_md:
Ornstein, Blasingame and Truscott (PSRM 2025, DOI 10.1017/psrm.2024.64) test few-shot prompts to GPT-3 and GPT-4 on four political text tasks. The tasks are sentiment in 945 SCOTUS tweets, tone in 935 campaign ads, ideology in 18,263 sentences from UK manifestos, and virtue-topic labels for 9,565 House one-minute speeches. On the tweets, GPT-3 got 88.4% of negative/positive signs right, against 64.3% for TweetNLP, 57.7% for Naive Bayes and 38.3% for the best dictionary. On ideology, LLM scores correlate with expert scores at rho 0.92 (economic) and 0.80 (social) across the 18 manifestos. LLM topic labels beat three random intruders in 80% of 400 blinded checks, where chance is 25%. Costs dropped about 1000-fold compared with crowd coding.

Three method points matter more than the headline numbers:
- Continuous measures are built from the label probability vector, not the argmax label.
- GPT-4, tuned with human feedback (RLHF), is overconfident. For over 70% of posts it put more than 99% on one label, and it chose Neutral more often than the human coders.
- Validation runs in three steps: tune the prompt on one hand-labelled set, check it on a second, then apply.

The authors also warn that the GPT-3 models they used were retired in January 2024, so the results cannot be reproduced.

For Paul's system, the paper does not bear on networks, money or allocation. It bears on the stance and text layer. Melange already supplies outside context in the prompt for its Claude stance rater, and it caches LLM outputs by model. The gaps are elsewhere:
- run_stage5.R throws away DEBATE's per-label probabilities and keeps only a sign, which is then multiplied by dictionary intensity.
- The Claude rater reports a confidence it states itself, not a calibrated probability.
- Regex topic routing has never been checked against human labels.
- The tweet gold queue puts the model's labels next to the human gold columns.

The paper measures sentiment toward court rulings, not stance toward a target, so its accuracy figures should not be read as an expected accuracy for CU stance.

bearings.paper_claim: Continuous measures built from the LLM's label probability vector track expert codes. The per-sentence score P(Conservative) minus P(Liberal), averaged per manifesto, gives rho 0.92 (economic) and 0.80 (social) across 18 UK manifestos, 1987-2010. Tweet sentiment uses the first principal component of the positive/neutral/negative probabilities.
bearings.system_side: Stage 5 collapses DEBATE output to an argmax sign. press_value = stance_sign x LSD intensity (run_stage5.R:9). final_sign takes either the bill sign or stance_sign (run_stage5.R:140). p_support, p_oppose and p_neutral are carried as columns (run_stage5.R:98,166) but never enter the aggregate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The comparison is approximate. The paper's evidence comes from GPT-3 next-token probabilities on a few-shot prompt, validated between parties on 18 documents. DEBATE runs with multi_label=True (stage5_debate.py:65), so its three entailment scores are independent and do not sum to 1. A p_support minus p_oppose contrast can still be defined, but it is a different object. It would have to beat sign x LSD on the 760-row press gold in a pre-registered single look. Until a second path reproduces it, the idea stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#press_value aggregate and human-label overlay|press_value aggregate and human-label overlay]]

bearings.paper_claim: Tweets whose meaning depends on outside political context are misread unless the prompt supplies that context. The sentiment prompt included a preamble describing each ruling, and the model reached 88.4% correct sign on 945 tweets.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.1, p.267-268; limitations on outside context
bearings.system_side: The Claude rater's system prompt carries the credit-union policy map and tells the model to judge by underlying interest. One example: a champion of the Credit Card Competition Act counts as oppose even when the text never says 'credit union'. It serves as the pre-labeller and as the third member of the ensemble.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's task is sentiment toward a court ruling, not stance toward an interest. The brain treats sentiment and stance as different things, so the paper supports the context-preamble design but gives no accuracy figure for CU stance. The paper also used few-shot examples, while claude_stance.py is zero-shot with a policy map.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader|Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader]]

bearings.paper_claim: GPT-4, tuned with RLHF, is poorly calibrated. For over 70% of posts it gave a single label more than 99% probability, and it returned Neutral more often than the authors did. GPT-4 was slightly worse than GPT-3 on sentiment, and newer models did not reliably improve on any task.
bearings.system_side: The Claude rater asks the model for a stated confidence from 0 to 1 inside its JSON reply (claude_stance.py:25). It defaults the stance to neutral, with confidence 0.0, when a call fails or returns an unrecognised label (claude_stance.py:80,89-91). It uses an RLHF chat model (default claude-sonnet-4-6, line 32).
bearings.transfer_conditions: These are GPT-3 and GPT-4 results, not Claude results. The Anthropic API returns no token log-probabilities, so the paper's calibrated probability-vector method cannot be applied to this rater. claude_conf should therefore not be treated as a probability. Neutral rows created by errors inflate the neutral class and should be counted apart from model-chosen neutral rows. This bears on the open question of how much of the reported 87.2% DEBATE-vs-Claude agreement reflects human agreement.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader|Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader]]

bearings.paper_claim: Dictionary methods lose badly when meaning depends on context. The best dictionary got 38.3% of tweet signs right, against 88.4% for GPT-3. 5,332 speeches contain the word 'honor', but GPT-3 labels only 145 as praising honor.
bearings.system_side: LSD2015 is used only for intensity (|net|/words), with negation phrases stripped first. Direction comes from the NLI and Claude stance readers, which keeps stance and tone separate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper measured dictionary error on direction, which the system already takes from a contextual model, so that design choice is consistent with the paper. The paper did not test dictionary intensity. Intensity inherits the same blindness to context: ceremonial or quoted language reads as 'heated'. The component's open question, whether LSD intensity correlates with human-coded intensity, is still untested.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity|Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity]]

bearings.paper_claim: LLM topic labels can be validated cheaply with an optimal-label task. A blinded coder picked GPT-3's label over three random intruders in 80% of 400 speeches, against 25% chance. Keyword presence badly overcounts a topic: 5,332 speeches contain 'honor', but only 145 praise it.
bearings.system_side: Release and post categories are assigned by regex keyword patterns (CATKW = MR.RAW_PATTERNS). These categories drive both the media blend and the press pillar's category weights. The component's open question asks for the precision of regex tagging against human coding.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's labels are open-ended virtue labels for US House one-minute speeches from 2013-2014. Melange uses fixed CU policy categories on press releases and posts. The intruder-task protocol transfers directly as a measurement check on existing regex tags; adopting LLM-assigned categories is a separate decision. The R scraper's CATEGORIES regex was not opened for this review.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-legislative-data#Release category taxonomy and billstatus synthetic rows|Release category taxonomy and billstatus synthetic rows]]

bearings.paper_claim: The recommended validation has three steps: hand-label a small set to design the prompt, validate on a second hand-labelled set, then apply. Hand labels are the independent criterion. The paper also notes that crowd workers increasingly use LLMs themselves (Veselovsky et al. 2023), which threatens how independent crowd codes are.
bearings.system_side: The tweet gold queue writes model_stance and model_margin, plus an api_* pre-label block, into the same rows as the human gold_* columns. Low-margin and anti-bank hard cases are deliberately oversampled. The gold-set component assumes that gold labels are independent of the pipeline.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper does not test anchoring on pre-labels, so this is a design implication, not a measured effect. If the labeller saw model_stance or api_* values, accuracy against these gold labels partly measures agreement with the model. Because hard slices are oversampled, Melange accuracies are not comparable with the paper's random-sample 88.4%.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-validation#Gold-set validation and zero-rank-delta gate|Gold-set validation and zero-rank-delta gate]]

bearings.paper_claim: Results from closed, vendor-served models can become impossible to reproduce. The GPT-3 models behind the paper's results were removed from the public API in January 2024.
bearings.system_side: The signed member-reference valence pass records which model scored each cached row (_cache_models) and stores resp.model and response_id with every classification. The agency/communion persona reader also keeps separate caches per model so that outputs from different instruments never mix (agency_communion_llm.py:24-28).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Caching keeps the outputs auditable after a model is retired, but scores cannot be regenerated, and a re-score on a successor model is a new instrument. Both layers are display-only or blend at low weight, so the reproducibility risk is bounded. The paper's warning carries over directly because both pipelines depend on Anthropic-served models.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-sna#Co-appearance and signed member-reference layers (display only)|Co-appearance and signed member-reference layers (display only)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Few-shot LLM classification can match or beat crowd and expert coding, but only when it is checked against hand labels the prompt was not tuned on. Results depend heavily on prompt design.
bearings.system_side: The persona channel classifies sentence-level cues with a few-shot codebook (strong cue 1.0, weak 0.5) and blends them at PERSONA_W 0.30. Its recorded validation is a functional gate (18/18) and a party signature, with no held-out human-gold accuracy for the cue labels.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper validated measures at the document level against expert and crowd codes. Here cues are classified per sentence and then aggregated per member. The paper's protocol would need a hand-coded cue sample that was not used to write the codebook. PERSONA_W 0.30 is kept by owner ruling, and nothing here argues for changing it.

gaps_exposed: Probability-based continuous stance is unused. DEBATE's p_support and p_oppose are written but not aggregated (run_stage5.R:98,140), and press_value takes direction from an argmax sign alone.
The Claude stance rater has no calibrated probabilities: its confidence is stated by the model in its JSON reply, and API errors silently become neutral at confidence 0 (claude_stance.py:80,89-91).
The regex category router (CATKW, build_media_blend.py:50) has no human-label validation. The paper's 400-item intruder task is a ready, cheap protocol for this.

Gold queues put model_stance and api_* pre-labels next to the gold_* columns (build_tweet_gold_queue.py:92-96). Nothing records whether gold labelling was blind to the model, so the assumption that gold is independent of the pipeline is untested.
No plan exists for retiring a model. The caches keep outputs, but no documented rule says how a successor model's scores are bridged or re-validated before they replace cached ones.
flags: The paper measures SENTIMENT toward SCOTUS rulings, not target-specific STANCE. The brain separates sentiment from stance, so do not quote the 88.4% figure as an expected accuracy for CU stance.
The paper's numbers come from GPT-3 and GPT-4 (2023-2024 API), and GPT-3 was retired in January 2024. Its figures cannot be reproduced and say nothing directly about Claude or DEBATE.

The cost figures ($0.60 vs $565.20; $2.50 vs about $3,226.70) are OpenAI prices from that period. They describe the window and denominator stated in the paper (935 ads; 18,263 sentences), not Melange's current costs.

Any re-scoring proposed here (a probability-contrast stance, LLM categories) is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). Any replacement of a live reader needs a pre-registered single look against held-out gold.
Possible conflict with the gold-set assumption that gold labels are independent of the pipeline: the tweet gold queue shows model outputs next to the gold columns.
Nothing in the paper touches the rejected SNA proposals, LDA edges, reciprocity, graph-rank or influence wording.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotations on this paper. His position on the stance components endorses LLM and transformer extraction (Kim J. 2025, Birkenmaier and Lechner 2025) and calls SVM baselines outdated. The paper broadly agrees: GPT-3 beat a fine-tuned RoBERTa (TweetNLP) and Naive Bayes on tweet sentiment. It adds two cautions his notes lack. First, newer RLHF models (GPT-4) were overconfident and no better. Second, every LLM measure needs separate hand-labelled validation. Paul's preference is partly stale against the system's own record: on the member-grouped held-out test, LinearSVC on TF-IDF scored 83.9%, against 0.757 reported for the transformer. The paper's 88.4% is a sentiment task, not CU stance. His noted weakness, that ambiguous statements are hard to untangle, matches the paper's finding that context-dependent items fail unless the prompt supplies context. The system's Claude rater already supplies that context.

related.why: Both papers validate few-shot LLM coding of political text against human gold. Birkenmaier supplies the codebook and Krippendorff-alpha framework used by the persona channel; Ornstein supplies the three-step prompt-validation protocol and the calibration warning.
Kim uses GPT-4 labels for interest-group positions on lobbying reports (96.9% vs human); Ornstein shows the same few-shot approach on four other text tasks and documents GPT-4's overconfidence.
Khan compares fine-tuned RoBERTa with classical models for political tweet stance; Ornstein uses a RoBERTa tweet model (TweetNLP) as the baseline that few-shot GPT-3 beats on sentiment.

Rice and Zorn argue that corpus-specific dictionaries fix the failures of general dictionaries on specialised vocabulary. Ornstein shows a dictionary at 38.3% against GPT-3 at 88.4% and argues that context, not vocabulary, is the binding problem.
Haselmayer combines a dictionary with crowd coding; Ornstein benchmarks LLMs against exactly that crowd-coding route and reports about a 1000-fold cost reduction.
Both use LLMs for political stance and sentiment classification; Dai adds logic-tensor constraints where Ornstein relies on few-shot prompting with probability-vector outputs.
